chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about tawhid. I said: 'Can I conceive of Him as a thing?' He said: 'Yes, without [being] comprehended by reason and without limit. So whatever your imagination falls upon from a thing — He is different from it. Nothing resembles Him, nor can the imaginations grasp Him. How can the imaginations grasp Him when He is different from what is conceived by reason and different from what is pictured in the imaginations? Rather, you can only imagine a thing [that is] beyond reason and without limits.'

key_terms.الأوهام: al-Awham — plural of wahm; imagination, faculty of conception, mental representations; here used to denote the limitations of human cognitive faculties
key_terms.التوحيد: Tawhid — Divine Unity/Oneness of God; the central theological concept in Islam
key_terms.خلاف: khilaf — contrary to, different from, opposite of
key_terms.محدود: mahdud — bounded, limited; having defined limits or boundaries
key_terms.معقول: ma'qul — that which is comprehended/perceived by reason ('aql); rational cognition

ai.seo_question: Can God be conceived or imagined according to Shia Islam? What does Imam al-Baqir teach about tawhid?
ai.summary: In this hadith, Imam al-Baqir (AS) responds to a question about tawhid — specifically whether God can be conceived as a 'thing'. The Imam's answer is subtly affirmative but immediately qualifies it: yes, God is a 'thing,' but unlike any thing that the mind can grasp or limit. The Imam establishes that whatever the imagination conceives, God is different from it, and that the very faculty of imagination cannot reach Him. This teaching reflects the classical Shia theological doctrine of divine transcendence (tanzih), which holds that God is beyond all human categories of thought. The early Muslim communities and scholars hearing this would recognize it as a refutation of anthropomorphist tendencies while affirming that God is not mere nothingness — He exists, but as a 'thing' beyond rational comprehension.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yaqoub, from Ali Bin Ibrahim, from Muhammad Bin Isa, from Abdul Rahman Bin Abu Najran who said,

‘I asked Abu Ja’farasws about the Tawheed (Oneness of Allahazwj), and I said, ‘Can I think of Himazwj as a thing?’ So heasws said: ‘Yes, without reasoning and no limit. So whatever your imagination occurs upon from a thing, so Heazwj is different to it. Nothing resembles Himazwj, nor can the imaginations grasp Himazwj. How can the imaginations grasp Himazwj and Heazwj is different to what is thought of and different to what is pictured in the imaginations? But rather, you can imagine something without reasoning and no limits’.
en.sarwar: 1. Muhammad ibn Ya‘qub has narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn ‘isa from ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn abu Najran who said the following.

“I asked Imam abu ‘Abdallah about the Oneness of Allah saying, ‘Can I think of Him (the creator) as a thing?’” The Imam replied, “Yes, but not as something well understood and clearly defined with in limits. What may become a subject of your thoughts is different from Him. Nothing resembles Him and the thoughts and imaginations can not reach Him. He is different from what can become the subject of thoughts and is different from whatever that can be perceived in ones thoughts. You can think of Him as some thing but not well understood and clearly defined (under certain limits).”
